abstract: The cervix is a dynamic mucosal barrier in the female reproductive tract that balances inflammatory and anti inflammatory functions to regulate physiologically critical functions, including pregnancy, sperm transport, fertility, and protection of the upper reproductive tract from infection. Despite its central role in reproduction, the cellular and transcriptional organization of the healthy human cervix remains incompletely characterized, including how clinical sampling methods influence the epithelial populations recovered and how cervical mucociliary programs compare with those of pulmonary epithelium. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNAseq) on paired Tischler punch biopsy and endocervical curettage (ECC) samples from four healthy, exogenous hormone-naive donors to generate a dedicated transcriptomic map of the healthy human cervix followed by an integrative computational analysis framework combining differential expression, functional enrichment, cell to cell communication, cross-tissue mapping, and regulon activity inference. This approach identified ten cell types spanning epithelial, stromal, vascular, and immune cell populations and found that sampling method strongly influenced cellular composition and transcriptional state as Tischler punch biopsy preferentially recovered basal and suprabasal epithelial populations, whereas ECC enriched for secretory and ciliated epithelial cell types. Cross-tissue comparison with publicly available healthy lung epithelial transcriptomics dataset revealed conserved mucociliary cell types alongside tissue-divergent transcriptional programs, including distinct regulation of ion transport and mucin associated genes. Together, these findings demonstrate the importance of sampling modality in resolving cervical epithelial heterogeneity, and reveal tissue-specialized mucociliary regulatory programs underlying cervical mucus biology and fertility regulation.
